newsitem.title: USA: Autos, Third Sector key to US-Japan insurance pact.
newsitem.headline: Autos, Third Sector key to US-Japan insurance pact.

text.p: Automobile insurance pricing and the entry of Japanese firms into the so-called "Third Sector" are the key sticking points in the deadlocked U.S.-Japan insurance talks, trade officials said on Saturday.

The two countries ended a two-day meeting in San Francisco without a breakthrough and said they were far apart on key issues, despite their pledge to resolve their differences by Dec. 15 on how to open up Japan's insurance market.

"We are still far apart on what should constitute substantial primary-sector deregulation and the measures needed to prevent a 'radical change' in the Third Sector," said Ira Shapiro, who headed the Washington team at the talks.

U.S. firms want the freedom to differentiate on the "basis of rate" so that they can offer competitive products -- for instance, by offering different premiums for men and women or for different regions.

While Japanese car insurers already charge different premiums based on age groups, Eisuke Sakakibara, the chief negotiator for Tokyo, said too much segmentation would defeat the purpose of insurance and could cause social problems.
"There will not be a 'liberalization' that conflicts with the basic rules of insurance," Sakakibara said.

Asked if the Finance Ministry thought the U.S. insurance industry was having such social problems, ministry officials said laws were different in each state and that there have been some lawsuits alleging discrimination.
The "third sector" -- as opposed to the primary life and property-and-casualty sectors -- covers personal accident, illness and nursing care, such as stand-alone cancer policies.
It has been a stronghold of foreign firms, but Washington fears this relatively small niche market could be saturated if Japanese insurance giants stampeded into the arena.
Washington has insisted on imposing a moratorium of a few years after a viable primary-sector deregulation so that foreign firms could prepare to compete with domestic titans.

But Sakakibara said Japan wanted to open up this sector immediately, taking various measures to avoid "radical changes" in the sector. He added that if no agreement could be reached by Dec. 15, Japanese firms would start Third Sector business from Jan. 1, 1997.
In such an event, Washington could impose retaliatory sanctions.
"If there are actions taken (by the Japanese) after that time (year-end) in the absence of an agreement, then we'll respond appropriately at that point," Shapiro said.

Officials said decisions at the ministerial level was needed to reach an agreement by the Dec. 15 target. No date for a top-level meeting has been set, but officials said they would meet further to lay ground for a showdown.
